'''Janet Guthrie''' (born March 7, 1938) is an American former [[racing driver]]. She is the first female to qualify and race in either the [[Indianapolis 500]], or the [[Daytona 500]], both of which she competed in during 1977. She had first attempted to enter the [[Indianapolis 500]] in 1976 but failed to qualify. She raced in three Indianapolis 500s: 1977 through 1979. She is also the first woman to lead a lap in [[NASCAR Cup Series]] competition.

Guthrie was originally an [[Aerospace engineering|aerospace engineer]], and after graduating from the [[University of Michigan]] with a physics degree in 1960, she worked with [[Republic Aviation]].<ref name="indystar.com">{{cite news|last=Litman|first=Laken| url=http://www.indystar.com/story/sports/motor/indy-500/2017/05/26/sleeping-her-car-indy-500-how-janet-guthrie-changed-racing-women/347958001/|title= From sleeping in her car to the Indy 500: How Janet Guthrie changed racing for women|work=[[The Indianapolis Star]] |date= May 26, 2017|access-date= August 7, 2017}}</ref> She got the 2024 NASCAR Landmark award on January 19, 2024.

== Racing career ==

Guthrie began racing in 1963 on the [[Sports Car Club of America|SCCA]] circuit in a [[Jaguar XK140]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.iop.org/careers/working-life/profiles/page_60280.html |title=Once a physicist: Janet Guthrie |publisher=[[Institute of Physics]] |date=n.d. |access-date=August 7, 2017 |archive-date=May 25, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190525172603/http://www.iop.org/careers/working-life/profiles/page_60280.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and by 1972, she was racing on a full-time basis. Her sportscar racing career included two class wins in the famed [[12 Hours of Sebring]] endurance race.<ref name="espnW"/>

In the 1976 [[World 600]], Guthrie finished fifteenth, becoming the first woman to compete in a NASCAR [[Winston Cup]] [[superspeedway]] race. Guthrie would go on to compete in four more races that season. The following season, she competed in her first [[1977 Daytona 500|Daytona 500]], finishing twelfth when her car's engine blew two cylinders with ten laps to go. For her performance in the race, though, she still earned the honor of Top Rookie. Overall, Guthrie went on to compete in 33 races in NASCAR over four seasons.<ref name=espn/> Her highest finish, sixth place at [[Bristol Motor Speedway|Bristol]] in 1977, is the best finish by a woman in a top-tier NASCAR race in the modern era, now currently tied with [[Danica Patrick]] in 2014.<ref name=espn>{{cite web|last=McGee |first=Ryan |title=Janet Guthrie outraced insults to make history |url=http://espn.go.com/espnw/more-sports/8963949/espnw-janet-guthrie-outraced-insults-make-auto-racing-history |work=[[ESPN.com#ESPNW|espnW]] |publisher=[[ESPN]] |access-date=February 24, 2013 |date=February 20, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130224010558/http://espn.go.com/espnw/more-sports/8963949/espnw-janet-guthrie-outraced-insults-make-auto-racing-history |archive-date=February 24, 2013 }}</ref>

[[Image:GuthrieWildcat.jpg|thumb|left|250px|Janet Guthrie's Wildcat 3-DGS, which she drove to ninth place in the [[1978 Indianapolis 500]]]]

Guthrie qualified for and competed in the [[1977 Indianapolis 500]], in a car entered by Rolla Vollstedt, but finished 29th with engine troubles. She would compete in two more Indianapolis 500s, finishing ninth in the [[1978 Indianapolis 500|1978 race]] while driving with a fractured wrist (injured in a charity tennis event two days earlier) she hid from race officials.<ref name="espnW">{{cite news|last1=Fabrizio |first1=Tony |title=Janet Guthrie: Racing's reluctant trailblazer is 'Qualified' |url=https://www.espn.com/espnw/culture/story/_/id/26777609/racing-reluctant-trailblazer-qualified |access-date=June 1, 2019 |work=[[ESPN.com#ESPNW|espnW]] |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=May 27, 2019}}</ref> Overall, she competed in 11 [[Indy car]] events with a best finish of fifth. During her unsuccessful bid to qualify for the [[1976 Indianapolis 500|1976 race]], many of the drivers in the male-dominated sport stated that the reason she did not qualify was mainly due to her sex.<ref name="espnW"/> These comments angered then three-time race winner [[A. J. Foyt]] to the point he lent Guthrie a back-up car to conduct a shake-down test. Her top practice lap in Foyt's car would have been adequate to qualify for the field.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Martin|first= Bruce|url=https://www.si.com/more-sports/2011/05/26/women-indy500 |title=From Guthrie to Patrick, women have made progress at Indy 500|magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]]|date= May 26, 2011|access-date=August 7, 2017}}</ref> She was unable to obtain funding through corporate sponsorship, and was forced into retirement.<ref>{{cite book|last=Guthrie|first= Janet|title=Janet Guthrie: A Life at Full Throttle|date= March 9, 2005|isbn=978-1894963312|page=382|publisher= Sport Media Pub.}}</ref><ref name="latimes">{{cite news|last=Dodds|first=Tracy|url= https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1987-05-24-sp-2407-story.html |title=THE INDIANAPOLIS 500 : Why Aren't Women Racing at Indy? Ask Guthrie|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|date=May 24, 1987|access-date=August 7, 2017}}</ref>

Nevertheless, Guthrie's place in history was secure. In 1979, the [[Supersisters]] trading card set was produced and distributed; one of the cards featured Guthrie's name and picture.<ref>{{cite news|last=Wulf |first=Steve |url=https://www.espn.com/espnw/news-commentary/story/_/id/12535055/original-roster |title=Supersisters: Original Roster |work=[[ESPN]] |date=March 23, 2015 |access-date=June 4, 2015}}</ref> Guthrie's helmet and race suit can be found in the [[Smithsonian Institution]] and she was one of the first elected to the [[International Women's Sports Hall of Fame]].<ref name="espnW"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://alumni.umich.edu/michigan-alumnus/firmly-in-the-drivers-seat/ |title=Firmly in the Driver's Seat|publisher=University of Michigan Alumni Association|first=Steve |last=Zoski| date=Winter 2019–20| access-date=August 23, 2020}}</ref> She was inducted into the [[International Motorsports Hall of Fame]] on April 27, 2006. Her 2005 autobiography, ''Janet Guthrie: A Life at Full Throttle'', has received critical praise from such publications as ''[[Sports Illustrated]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.motorsportshalloffame.com/Hall-of-Fame-Members/Bio.aspx?q=Janet%20Guthrie|title=Janet Guthrie Bio|publisher=[[International Motorsports Hall of Fame]]|date=2017|access-date=August 7, 2017|archive-date=February 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190214045952/http://www.motorsportshalloffame.com/Hall-of-Fame-Members/Bio.aspx?q=Janet%20Guthrie|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Battling sexism in motorsports==
In a groundbreaking interview with Tracy Dodds for the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' in 1987, Guthrie lamented the lack of corporate sponsorships for female drivers:<ref name="latimes" />
{{Blockquote
|text=Men are getting sponsorship and women can’t. That sounds unfair. But who cares about unfair? What counts is the bottom line. Sponsors want the publicity that racing brings. But a successful woman driver will get ten times the attention that a man will get. So, now, what really is important? It keeps coming back to the good ol’ boy network. A lot of corporations are spending a lot of tax deductible dollars to sponsor male racing drivers.
}}

The struggle for female drivers to secure corporate sponsorships continued. When [[Pippa Mann]] lacked the funding to enter the Indianapolis 500 in 2020 despite driving the previous year, the 2020 race was left with no women drivers. Guthrie said she was unlikely to watch the 2020 race due to her disappointment.<ref name="charlotte">{{cite news|url=https://www.charlotteobserver.com/sports/nascar-auto-racing/article245164145.html|title=There are no women in this year's Indy 500. The troubling reasons why center on sexism|first=Alex|last=Andrejev|date=August 22, 2020|access-date=August 23, 2020|work=[[The Charlotte Observer]]}}</ref> Guthrie herself initially said she was hesitant to address sexism in motorsports, but her mindset changed after she qualified for her first Indianapolis 500 in 1977 and was part of the downtown parade. As Guthrie described, “There were these guys who had little girls on their shoulders and were sort of waving these little girls as if I represented hope for the future."<ref name="charlotte" />

In 2011, Guthrie signed a petition in support of the [[Women to drive movement|right of women in Saudi Arabia to drive]].<ref name="beast">{{Cite news|url=https://www.thedailybeast.com/articles/2011/06/17/saudi-arabian-women-plan-day-of-protest-by-driving-on-june-17|title=Saudi Arabian Women Plan Day of Protest by Driving on June 17|last=Keyes|first=David| work=[[The Daily Beast]]|date=June 17, 2011|access-date=July 4, 2019|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://theworld.org/stories/2013/08/14/women-drivers-and-king|first=Marco|last= Werman|title=Women drivers and the king|work=[[Public Radio International]]| language=en|date=January 17, 2011|access-date=July 4, 2019}}</ref> The petition called on Saudi [[Abdullah of Saudi Arabia|King Abdullah]] to sponsor a Saudi Women's Grand Prix. The project was the idea of human rights activist [[David Keyes]].<ref name="beast" />

''Qualified'', an episode of [[ESPN]] [[30 for 30]] covering her racing career, aired on May 28, 2019 (Volume III, Episode 29). In it, she says, "You can go back to antiquity to find women doing extraordinary things, but their history is forgotten. Or denied to have ever existed. So women keep reinventing the wheel. Women have always done these things, and they always will."<ref name="espnW"/>

In 2019, Guthrie was inducted into the [[Automotive Hall of Fame]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.automotivehalloffame.org/honoree/janet-guthrie/|title= Janet Guthrie| publisher=[[Automotive Hall of Fame]]|access-date=July 24, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190724194356/https://www.automotivehalloffame.org/honoree/janet-guthrie/|archive-date=July 24, 2019|url-status=dead}}</ref> for her achievements in motorsports. She is the 5th woman to be inducted.

==Personal life==
Guthrie was born in [[Iowa City, Iowa]] to Jean Ruth Guthrie (née Midkiff) and William Lain Guthrie, both pilots.<ref name="indystar.com" /> She is the oldest of five children. Her family moved to [[Miami]], [[Florida]] when Janet was three years old after her father accepted a job with [[Eastern Air Lines]]. Janet herself earned her pilot's license at 17 years old.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/sports/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/guthrie-janet|title=Janet Guthrie|publisher=[[Encyclopedia.com]]|access-date=August 23, 2020}}</ref>

Guthrie married Warren Levine, a charter airline pilot, in 1989.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.aspentimes.com/news/warren-levine/|title=Warren Levine|date=January 5, 2007|work=[[The Aspen Times]]}}</ref> He died on December 30, 2006, of a sudden heart attack.<ref name="indystar.com"/>

A feature film about Guthrie starring Hillary Swank was announced in 2021.<ref>{{cite web | last=Bupp | first=Phillip | title=Hilary Swank to play Indy 500 trailblazer Janet Guthrie in feature film | website=Awful Announcing | date=2021-05-07 | url=https://awfulannouncing.com/racing/hilary-swank-to-play-indy-500-trailblazer-janet-guthrie-in-feature-film.html | access-date=2026-05-14}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==

Guthrie has been inducted into the following halls of fame:
* [[International Women's Sports Hall of Fame]] (1980)
* [[International Motorsports Hall of Fame]] (2006)
* [[Indianapolis Motor Speedway Museum#Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame|Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame]] (2006)
* [[Automotive Hall of Fame]] (2019)
* [[NASCAR Hall of Fame]] (2024)
* [[Motorsports Hall of Fame of America]] (2021)
